The iTARFlow surrogate generates stochastic trajectories and evaluates their
continuous probability density. This makes it useful when you need both samples
and a surrogate likelihood for [parameter inference](../sbi/vi-mcmc.qmd).
It currently accepts static inputs only.

## Try it

This small continuous-valued example uses 40 parameter settings, four
realisations per setting and eight time points. The response is
$y(t)=\theta(1+\sin t)+0.3\cos t+\epsilon$, with independent
$\epsilon\sim N(0,0.08^2)$. The known mean lets us see what the surrogate learns.
This is a short teaching fit, not a benchmark of the model families.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Create the example bank"
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from metis import SimulationDataset, Surrogate, TrainingConfig

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
times = np.linspace(0, 2, 8)
inputs = np.repeat(np.linspace(0.2, 1.2, 40)[:, None], 4, axis=0)
mean = inputs[:, None, :] * (1 + np.sin(times)[None, :, None])
mean = mean + 0.3 * np.cos(times)[None, :, None]
outputs = mean + rng.normal(0, 0.08, mean.shape)
bank = SimulationDataset.from_arrays(
    inputs, outputs, input_names=["theta"], output_names=["response"], times=times,
)
split = bank.split(seed=42)
```

```{python}
model = Surrogate(
    "itarflow",
    model_options={"channels": 32, "num_blocks": 2, "num_layers": 1, "num_heads": 2},
).fit(
    split.train, split.validation,
    config=TrainingConfig(steps=300, batch_size=32, eval_every=50, seed=42),
)
```

Generate 100 trajectories at one held-out parameter setting. The shaded band
shows pointwise 5th–95th percentiles of these draws; it represents the fitted
model's variability, not uncertainty in its fitted weights.

```{python}
theta = split.test.inputs[:1]
draws = model.sample(theta, n_samples=100, seed=13)[0, :, :, 0]
expected = theta[0, 0] * (1 + np.sin(times)) + 0.3 * np.cos(times)
print("Draws × time points:", draws.shape)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot generated trajectories"
#| fig-cap: "iTARFlow: short CPU fit on the synthetic continuous bank. The shaded band contains the middle 90% of surrogate draws at each time."
low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.fill_between(times, low, high, alpha=0.25, label="Surrogate 90% band")
ax.plot(times, draws[:8].T, color="C0", alpha=0.15, linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(times, draws.mean(axis=0), color="C0", label="Surrogate sample mean")
ax.plot(times, expected, "--", color="black", label="Known mean")
ax.plot(times, split.test.outputs[0, :, 0], "o", color="C1", label="Held-out realisation")
ax.set(xlabel="Time", ylabel="Response")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For a real bank, assess coverage over many held-out settings using the
[evaluation tools](../package/evaluation.qmd).

The density is also available in the original output units:

```{python}
log_density = model.log_prob(theta, split.test.outputs[:1])
print("Log density of the held-out trajectory:", log_density[0])
```

This is the fitted flow's density, not the simulator's exact likelihood or the
probability of a particular integer count.

## How it works

### Maximum likelihood via change of variables
A Normalising Flow parametrises an invertible transformation $f_{\theta}$ from the data distribution $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ to a noise distribution $p_0$ (usually Gaussian). Once trained the network can be inverted to transform noise samples into data. This transformation also has an associated density $p_{\mathrm{model}}$ which is accessible via the change of variable formula

$$
\log p_{\mathrm{model}}(x)=\log p_0(f_{\theta}(x))+\log\vert\mathrm{det}(\frac{df_{\theta}(x)}{dx})\vert
$$

Architecturally Normalising Flows are designed to be exactly invertible with log-determinants that can be efficiently computed. This allows a maximum likelihood estimation objective to be implemented as

$$
\min_{\theta}\; -\log p_0(f_{\theta}(x))-\log\vert\mathrm{det}(\frac{df_{\theta}(x)}{dx})\vert
$$


### Architecture

Normalising Flows have a rich literature with architectures that make different tradeoffs and until recently they were not regarded as scalable as generative models. Recently, the Transformer Autoregressive Flow (TARFlow) [@tarflow] has emerged as a scalable approach to Normalising Flows. Like many Normalising Flows the overall network $f_{\theta}$ is a composition of several invertible *blocks* $f_{M}\circ f_{M-1}\cdots\circ f_{1}$. Each of these blocks flips the order of the sequence with $\pi(x)$, and predicts scale $\alpha$ and shift $\mu$ parameters for each of the elements in the sequence with an autoregressive transformer $T(x)$:
$$
\begin{align}
&x^{\mathrm{output}}_{i}=(x^{\mathrm{input}}_{i}-\mu_{i})\odot \exp (-\alpha_i)\\
&\text{where } \mu_i \text{ and } \alpha_i \text{ are predicted by } T(x_{<i})\\
\end{align}
$$


::: {#fig-tar-block}
![](images/transformer-ar-flow-block.svg){fig-alt="An invertible transformer autoregressive flow block predicts scale and shift."}

Transformer Autoregressive Flow Block. Adapted from @tarflow.
:::

Crucially, since the transformer is causal, $\alpha_i$ and $\mu_i$ only depend on the elements strictly preceding $i$. Hence, the block can be exactly inverted by autoregressively rolling out

$$
x^{\mathrm{input}}_{i}=(x^{\mathrm{output}}_{i}\odot\exp(\alpha_i))+\mu_i
$$


Flow models can become numerically unstable on some datasets. METIS does not
apply the noise augmentation and Tweedie denoising used in the image experiments
of @tarflow; inspect samples and held-out densities on your own bank.

## Change its size

`channels` controls width, `num_blocks` the number of invertible blocks, and
`num_layers` the transformer layers per block. `num_heads` controls attention
heads and `num_static_tokens` controls static-input conditioning tokens.
The default uses width 64, two blocks, two layers and four heads/static tokens.

`patch_size` groups consecutive time points into one token. The default is one;
larger values reduce the sequence length but require a divisible time grid.

```bash
uv run metis train model=itarflow model.model_options.channels=128
```
